title: Run a stage beyond the Hub deployment
description: Understand sanitized invocations, completion modes and project-scoped callbacks for external workers.

chapters.title: Use a boundary, not the internal queue

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional customer with a processing service outside Hub's cluster. Should we connect it directly to the internal workflow queue?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the workflow forwarder boundary. It sends a smaller, versioned invocation to the customer's RabbitMQ destination or HTTPS endpoint, without exposing the internal run and storage credentials. The deployment must enable the forwarder and make its operation available.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does a custom workflow automatically borrow the deployment's broker settings?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Configure the intended customer destination explicitly, including the appropriate secure transport. Keep the workflow disabled until the worker and completion path are ready.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The invocation reaches the customer's queue. Is our analysis stage complete?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Only if delivery itself is the chosen outcome. Delivered mode completes after confirmed delivery. Callback mode keeps the stage open until the external result comes back. Use callback mode when downstream routing needs that returned result.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What helps if the same invocation arrives twice?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The execution identifier is the external idempotency key. Deduplicate work using it, and retain the operation and trace context. Signed media access is included only when the binding explicitly enables it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the external worker use its RabbitMQ password to return the result to Hub?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Broker credentials, Agent keys and callback authentication serve different purposes. Provision the documented short-lived access token for the correct tenant with only the required workflow-run update permission, and store it privately outside the workflow definition.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So no bearer token pasted into the designer or committed with an example?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Limit its lifetime and permissions, and rotate or revoke it if exposed. Use the invocation's callback destination rather than inventing a URL from a device name.

chapters.title: Return the right kind of result

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the important choice in the callback body?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Return exactly one output channel: routing values when your system owns the output, or a supported block payload when Hub should validate and persist it. The operation must match the invocation. Hub derives recording and ownership context from the stored run.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And an accepted callback proves everything is already visible?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not yet. Acceptance confirms the result was queued; block persistence is asynchronous. Retry identical transient failures with backoff, don't overwrite a different accepted result, and verify the final stored output before declaring the integration complete.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
